To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Adversarial Imitation can work well even for high-dimensional sparse reward tasks; (2) A minimal adversary (128 parameters) can learn to solve these tasks; (3) The adversary can be easily trained with the most basic GAIL formulation; (4) The adversary learns a useful reward signal that is better than staged dense reward signals; (5) The adversary is able to learn the task without any task reward signal, only from imitation
a minimal adversary, acting as a learned reward, can enable an agent to learn a task from video demonstrations and sparse rewards.

we show that adversarial learning can be used as a general-purpose tool to address a variety of problems in reinforcement learning, and can be used to solve a wide range of tasks, even in the presence of sparse and delayed reward.

The main takeaway from our work is that
adversarial imitation is a powerful tool to learn a useful world model and explore effectively even in the absence of dense reward signals.
a small, simple adversary can provide an effective reward signal for learning complex behaviors in a high dimensional space.
adversarial imitation learning can work well even with very small adversaries, and in fact, the smaller the adversary the more robust the agent is to distribution shift.
